source.title: Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model

digest.question: How can a flock move as one when no bird leads?

hookResult.text: Each bird follows a few simple rules about the birds near it, and the flock's motion emerges from them.

anchors.quote: The aggregate motion of the simulated flock is the result of the dense interaction of the relatively simple behaviors of the individual simulated birds.

causalChain.claim: Each bird perceives only the flockmates near it.

anchors.quote: an individual bird must have a localized and filtered perception of the rest of the flock.
the aggregate motion that we intuitively recognize as "flocking" (or schooling or herding) depends upon a limited, localized view of the world.

causalChain.claim: Each bird balances three behaviours: avoid collisions, match velocity, and stay near the flock's centre.

anchors.quote: 1. Collision Avoidance: avoid collisions with nearby flockmates
2. Velocity Matching: attempt to match velocity with nearby flockmates
3. Flock Centering: attempt to stay close to nearby flockmates

causalChain.claim: The flock's coordinated motion emerges from these local behaviours, with no leader.

anchors.quote: The aggregate motion of the simulated flock is the result of the dense interaction of the relatively simple behaviors of the individual simulated birds.
The aggregate motion of the simulated flock is created by a distributed behavioral model much like that at work in a natural flock; the birds choose their own course.

routing.reason: Reynolds' boids are agents that each steer by rules about their near neighbours, which the agents family's flock models directly.

counterfactual.prompt: What if birds ignored their neighbours' headings?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: Within 20 seconds this world's flock agrees on a heading far more than the other world's: its agreement is higher by more than half the scale.

beginner.text: Each bird turns to match the way its neighbours are flying. No bird leads.
beginner.analogy: Like people leaving a stadium: each matches the pace and direction of those beside them, and nobody is in charge.

intermediate.text: Each step, a bird steers toward the average heading of the birds it can see. Move together sets how hard it steers.

advanced.text: Aᵢ = w_a (ūᵢ − vᵢ): bird i accelerates toward ūᵢ, the mean velocity of the birds it sees, at rate w_a, which is Move together.

guide.idle: No bird leads. Each one steers only by the few it can see.

guide.lowered: You lowered Move together{to}, so birds care less which way their neighbours fly.

levels.title: Three urges, and the first: keep your distance
levels.goal: Change each bird's personal space, and watch the spacing.

anchors.quote: 1. Collision Avoidance: avoid collisions with nearby flockmates

counterfactual.prompt: What if birds never kept their distance?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: Without personal space the other world's flock bunches far tighter: after 20 seconds its birds sit more than half a world unit closer to their nearest neighbours.

beginner.text: A bird follows three urges: keep your distance, match your neighbours, stay with the flock. Personal space is the first. It stops collisions and sets how far apart birds fly.
beginner.analogy: Like people on a busy pavement, each keeping a step's distance from those around them.

intermediate.text: A bird steers away from any neighbour closer than its separation radius, 1.55 world units here. Personal space sets how quickly it steers away.

advanced.text: Sᵢ = w_s (v* sᵢ / |sᵢ| − vᵢ), where sᵢ sums −δᵢⱼ / |δᵢⱼ|² over the neighbours closer than R_s: a bird turns away from crowding, hardest from the nearest, at rate w_s, which is Personal space.

anchors.quote: 1. Collision Avoidance: avoid collisions with nearby flockmates
2. Velocity Matching: attempt to match velocity with nearby flockmates
3. Flock Centering: attempt to stay close to nearby flockmates

guide.raised: You gave each bird more personal space{to}, so it swerves sooner from a bird that comes too close.
guide.lowered: You shrank each bird's personal space{to}, so birds let others crowd in.
guide.atMinimum: At 0, birds do nothing to keep apart.

levels.title: Stay with the flock
levels.goal: Change how strongly birds stay close, and watch how far the flock spreads.

anchors.quote: 3. Flock Centering: attempt to stay close to nearby flockmates

counterfactual.prompt: What if birds had no urge to stay together?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: Without the pull toward the middle, the other world's flock spreads out across the valley: after 40 seconds its spread is more than 3 world units wider.

beginner.text: The third urge: steer toward the middle of the birds you can see. It keeps the flock compact instead of spreading across the valley.
beginner.analogy: Like friends in a crowd drifting back toward each other when they get separated.

intermediate.text: Each step, a bird steers toward the centre of the birds within its sight. Stay close sets how quickly. The ring on the ground shows the flock's spread: how far, on average, the birds of its largest group are from its centre.

advanced.text: Cᵢ = w_c (v* cᵢ / max(|cᵢ|, r_c) − vᵢ), where cᵢ is the mean offset to the birds bird i sees: it steers toward their centre at rate w_c, which is Stay close, easing off within r_c. The spread is the root-mean-square distance of the largest group's birds from its centre, the short way round.
advanced.equation: Cᵢ = w_c (v* cᵢ / max(|cᵢ|, r_c) − vᵢ)

anchors.quote: 3. Flock Centering: attempt to stay close to nearby flockmates

guide.lowered: You weakened the pull toward the middle{to}, so birds stop turning back.

levels.title: Does it behave like a flock?
levels.goal: Change how early birds swerve, and watch the flock pass the rocks.

anchors.quote: avoiding an obstacle should involve long-range planning rather than panicky corrections at the last minute.

counterfactual.prompt: What if birds had no rule for rocks?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: Without the rule, birds fly straight through the rocks: together they spend more than three times as long inside them as this world's birds.

difference.label: Time birds spend inside rocks over 20 seconds

beginner.text: One way to judge a flock model is to put rocks in its way and watch. A real flock never flies through a rock. Nothing in these rules mentions rocks except a push away from them.
beginner.analogy: Like a stream flowing round a stone and joining up again behind it.

intermediate.text: A bird is pushed away from a rock once it comes within this distance. Nothing else is added: how the flock parts and re-forms comes from the three urges.

advanced.text: Oᵢ = Σ w_o (R_o − |δᵢₒ|)(−δᵢₒ / |δᵢₒ|) over rocks closer than R_o: the push starts R_o from the rock and grows linearly toward it. The model's rocks push like a force field; they do not steer a bird away ahead of time.

anchors.quote: Real flocks sometimes split apart to go around an obstacle.
Solitary boids and smaller flocks join to become larger flocks, and in the presence of external obstacles (discussed below), larger flocks can split into smaller flocks.

guide.lowered: You made birds swerve late{to}, so they come close to the rocks before they turn.

levels.title: Order from the bottom up
levels.goal: Find the strength of Move together at which order appears.

counterfactual.prompt: What if the flock were a quarter as dense?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: The sparser flock takes far longer to agree: at least 10 seconds longer to reach agreement 0.8, if it gets there within 40 seconds at all.

beginner.text: Below some strength of following, the flock stays disordered. Above it, order appears, and the change comes over a fairly small range of the control. No bird plans it.
beginner.analogy: Like a crowd starting to clap in time: below some eagerness to follow it stays ragged, and above it a rhythm takes hold.

intermediate.text: Change Move together a little at a time and watch the compass's arrow. A steep rise in agreement over a small change of the control marks a change from disorder to order.

advanced.text: φ = |(1/N) Σ vᵢ / |vᵢ||, the directional agreement. A steep rise of φ over a small change of w_a marks a transition from disorder to order.

guide.lowered: You lowered Move together{to}, so each bird follows its neighbours less.
guide.atMinimum: At 0, no bird follows its neighbours at all.

levels.carryForward: Order can appear from local rules alone, once following is strong enough.

limits.text: A two-dimensional teaching adaptation of the paper's model, not a reproduction of its system or its results.
The rules are summed with weights and capped, a teaching choice; the levels say where that matters.
Rocks push birds like a force field rather than steering them away ahead of time.
Every level opens on one seed, chosen by a rule (ADR-0003). One run shows what these rules can do, not what they usually do.
